the Chinese economy is experiencing a major transformation of its technological regime, that this process is closely related to industrial restructuring, and that the new industrial system has a public character.

China has been successful in improving its technological capabilities and that the main source of the gains is the public sector.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the question of how a large, semi industrialized country with a socialist economy, which has been relatively isolated from the world economy for a long time, can achieve technological progress and catch up with the more developed economies.

two main issues: first, the role of the public sector in China’s technological catching-up process; second, the possibility for China’s public sector to achieve technological upgrading in the face of the growing presence in the Chinese market of large TNCs.

the following issues: (a) the impact of the reforms on China’s technological catching up; (b) the evolution of Chinese technological policy since the reforms and the role of foreign capital; (c) the relationship between the Chinese government and the enterprises; (d) the role of state-owned firms in technological upgrading; (e) the relationship between property rights and technological progress.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
China is not yet a “technological tiger” and is unlikely to be so for a long time to come.
China is a large country in which the socialist economy has not yet failed, and in which a large-scale and rapid process of industrialization and modernization is under way.

China’s experience in the past two decades has shown that a socialist economy is capable of achieving a substantial improvement in its technological performance, and that such an improvement is consistent with a radical reform of the public sector.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
China is not an “economic miracle” but a “technological success”.

, despite the many difficulties and problems encountered in the process of reform and opening, the Chinese government has succeeded in creating an institutional environment conducive to the rapid development of the country’s technological capacity and the upgrading of the industrial structure.

, despite the existence of many problems, China’s experience shows that a radical change in the ability of a socialist economy to achieve technical progress does not require a radical change in its property relations.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the Chinese experience is a good illustration of the fact that the development of a national innovation system is not the automatic product of market mechanisms, but a complex process which depends on a variety of institutional arrangements and policy choices.

the Chinese government has been able to combine its own efforts with the inflow of foreign technology and capital, in a way that is consistent with the preservation of public property and control of the economy.
the state-owned sector is not a burden on the economy, but rather the main engine of economic growth.
